To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

heading discrimination is (1) independent of movement direction in world (gravity) coordinates and (2) dependent on movement direction in body (head) coordinates and on body orientation relative to gravity.

(1) vestibular heading thresholds depend on movement direction relative to head coordinates, (2) vestibular heading discrimination is better in the upright orientation, and (3) heading thresholds are correlated with, but larger than, predictions from a coarse direction discrimination task

(1) vestibular heading discrimination depends on movement direction in the plane of the otoliths and on body orientation, but not on movement direction in space; (2) vestibular heading thresholds are significantly larger than coarse direction discrimination thresholds, but are correlated with them; and (3) the larger vestibular heading thresholds could be accounted for, at least in part, by an amplitude–nonlinearity in the representation of inertial acceleration.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the brain processes the vestibular cues to self-motion.
the ability to judge the direction of linear motion, i.e., the heading.
the neural mechanisms underlying the vestibular sense of heading.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

vestibular heading discrimination and sensitivity to inertial acceleration are best described in head-centered coordinates and depend on body orientation, but that they can be accounted for by a simple neural model.

the vestibular heading discrimination task involves both the otoliths and the semicircular canals, and that the otoliths provide a representation of the direction and magnitude of linear self-motion in head-centered coordinates, which is then used by the brain to compute heading.

heading discrimination thresholds are determined primarily by the otoliths' response to linear acceleration in head coordinates, but that the thresholds are larger than predicted based on the otoliths response to linear acceleration along the same axis because the otoliths respond nonlinearly to linear acceleration along that axis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the nervous system represents inertial acceleration as a linear combination of gravity, movement direction in head, and body orientation.
vestibular heading discrimination is best understood as a process that combines the direction and amplitude of movement in head-centered space, with a nonlinearity that is sensitive to amplitude.
the otolith organs provide a representation of linear motion in head coordinates, but that this representation is distorted by a nonlinearity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
vestibular heading discrimination depends on the direction of movement relative to the otololiths, but not on the direction of the movement relative to gravity.
vestibular heading thresholds depend on movement direction in the same coordinates as coarse direction discrimination thresholds.
the nervous system does not use the otoliths to estimate heading in world coordinates.
